analysis.one_liner: Sends families $3,000–$3,600 per child per year through a fully refundable child tax credit paid monthly.
analysis.headline: A child tax credit expansion of $3,000–$3,600 per child with 37 Senate cosponsors died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace today's child tax credit with a larger one: $3,000 per child and $3,600 for children under six, fully refundable so that families who owe little or no income tax still get the full amount. It would pay the credit out in monthly installments instead of a once-a-year refund, raise it with inflation each year, and extend an equivalent benefit to families in Puerto Rico and the other territories. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children under 17, especially low- and middle-income families who owe little or no federal income tax and therefore cannot currently use the full child tax credit. Under the bill they would receive the full $3,000–$3,600 per child regardless of tax liability, delivered monthly, with the same benefit extended to families in Puerto Rico and the U.S. territories.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially lower-income ones

how_it_helps.text: The bill replaces the current child tax credit with $3,000 per child (120% of that, or $3,600, for children under age 6), and makes the credit fully refundable so families with little or no income tax liability receive the full amount.
It directs the Treasury to set up a program to pay the credit out on a monthly basis during the year, rather than as a lump sum at tax time.
The credit amount would rise each year with inflation.
It adds a $500 credit for other dependents and extends equivalent payments to residents of Puerto Rico, the Northern Mariana Islands, and other U.S. territories.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, and ultimately taxpayers generally, who bear the cost of a much larger refundable credit. Some higher-income households would also receive less than under current law, because the credit phases down beginning at $130,000 for single filers and $180,000 for joint filers.

drawbacks.text: The bill's chief cost is fiscal: a much larger, fully refundable credit paid to tens of millions of families is a major federal expenditure, and the bill contains no offsetting revenue.
Families whose advance monthly payments exceed the credit they ultimately qualify for would have to repay the excess when they file their taxes, which can produce an unexpected bill.

A child or dependent without a taxpayer identification number issued by the filing deadline, or a taxpayer whose own ID number was issued late, cannot claim the credit, which excludes some mixed-status families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and broad: it reaches families that current law leaves out entirely and converts an annual refund into a monthly payment that can cover recurring costs like rent and food. The costs are real but ordinary ones for a public benefit — federal revenue and some added repayment complexity at tax time — and the bill includes anti-fraud disqualification rules and income phase-downs to limit them. On the merits it is a straightforward trade of federal money for lower child poverty, and it was never tested against that trade in any hearing or vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee took no action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it never reached the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet and 37 other senators introduced the American Family Act of 2019 on March 6, 2019.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the bill's history for the remainder of the 116th Congress — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.
All 37 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No family gained the credit because the bill never advanced. The status quo was preserved for the federal treasury and for higher-income households who would have seen their credits phase down at lower income thresholds; families who owed little or no income tax lost the chance at the full benefit.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its design of a fully refundable $3,000/$3,600 child credit with monthly advance payments.

for.name: 37 senators (36 Democrats and 1 Independent)
for.role: Senate cosponsors, including Sens. Brown, Booker, Harris, Sanders, Warren, and Democratic leader Schumer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired the committee to which it was referred.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: His committee, the sole committee of referral, took no action on the bill — no hearing, no markup — from its March 2019 referral through the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 37 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's single Independent, and no Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill; the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill phases the new credit down starting at $130,000 for single filers and $180,000 for joint filers, lower than current law's phase-out points, so many upper-income families would receive less than the current $2,000-per-child credit. Their gain under the status quo is a cost borne by the expanded support for lower-income families.
